text: Listen, Willie. Tomorrow's supply call. Can you not send over a few haggis?
The chef we have here, this is the kind of first thing...
Willie? Hello, Willie. Can you hear me? Over.
This is Charlie Rick to High Bannion Control. Are you receiving?
I say again, Charlie Rick to High Bannion Control. Do you read me? Over.
Good morning. Are you wanting a lift?
Hey, listen to that. That's how Ryan gets at it again.
OK, take it.
Three rigs destroyed in a month. Two of them ours, General.
Brigadier, actually.
Well, Brigadier, my company's lost millions.
The government is equally concerned, I can assure you, Mr Hargall.
More especially about the loss of life.
If this keeps up, there won't be a man left willing to work out there.
Do we have to put up with this hullabaloo?
I'm afraid we've rather imposed ourselves on the landlord.
If he wants to play his pipes, there's not much I can do about it.
Ah, Mr Benton, any news of the Doctor yet?
No, sir, nothing yet.
We'll put him to bed.
It'll materialise by now.
Mr Benton! Sir?
Is this thing still working? As far as I know, sir, yes.
You get on well with the landlord, don't you?
Yes, sir, I suppose I do.
We'll use your influence to get him to play the pipes when we're out.
Right, sir.
There's the Doctor now, sir. Good Lord!
Mr Hargall!
Who's the man in the driving seat?
Him. That's the Duke of Forgill, the local big shot.
He doesn't make things easy.
He owns just about everything on this part of Scotland,
except our shore base.
Frankly, he doesn't like us, not one little bit.
Oh, welcome back, Doctor. I want to know one thing, Brigadier.
What's that?
That, Doctor, is a kilt.
Suits you very well.
Oh, do you think so? Yes.
Oh, um, this is His Grace, the Duke of Forgill.
He very kindly gave us a lift.
I had to pass here on my way to the oil base.
To see me.
To see you, Mr Hickle. Hargall.
To complain yet again about your roughnecks
trespassing and poaching on my property.
My men have been warned, sir.
If any of them are caught, they'll be dismissed immediately.
Well, let me give you a final warning.
If my ghillie catches them on my land again, they'll be shot.
And that's no idle threat, Mr Hickle.
I'll be expecting you, Brigadier.
Yes, Mr Hickle.
I trust the Army isn't going to help those people?
Is that why you were sent here?
No, sir. We're a... a military investigation team.
Investigating what?
I'm afraid our mission is a sensitive matter, sir.
Official secrets and all that twaddly.
Well, I won't pry.
My family have served this country for seven centuries,
but that seems not to count these days, does it?
Good day to you.
An odd man. Rather medieval in his ideas.
A man of convictions.
All the same, he did save us a long walk, sir.
Anyway, it's nice to see you again, Brigadier.
And you, Miss Smith.
I didn't expect to see you in a kilt.
My dear Miss Smith, as you'll remember, my name is Lethbridge Stewart.
The Klan.
Oh, sorry. I thought you were doing a doctor.
It's an absurd idea.
Brigadier.
Why have you called me back?
I hope you've got a very good reason.
All three rigs were in this area.
Therefore, it seems to us...
Brigadier, Brigadier.
Have you brought me 270 million miles just to sort out a little trouble at sea?
Three serious disasters, Doctor.
When I left the psionic beam with you, Brigadier,
I said it was only to be used in an emergency.
This is an emergency.
Oh, an emergency?
Ha!
It's about time the people who run this planet of yours
realise that to be dependent upon a mineral slime just doesn't make sense.
Now, the energising of hydrogen...
Doctor, the destruction of these rigs is a complete mystery.
Do you want more men to die?
No.
Very well.
When do we start?
The oil company. We're paying them a visit this afternoon.
Here's a preliminary medical report on the condition of the bodies.
They died the same way as the others. Exposure and drowning.
Yes, so I heard, Mr Huckle.
There's quite a few crush injuries.
The rig collapsed.
I think I'd better take a look at these, sir.
Yes, good idea, Sullivan.
You cut off to the sick bay and we'll see you back at headquarters.
Aye, aye, sir.
I'll come with you as far as the village.
I can talk to some of the local people, see what I can find out, OK?
See you later.
Bye, Doctor.
You know, these things always remind me of three-legged spiders in Wellington boots.
Correction.
Concrete boots. Thousands of tons of it.
Those babies are meant to be unscathed.
Unsinkable.
Yes, so was the Bismarck, and we all know that story.
We spent a fortune proving the Waverley Field geologically sound.
Everything is constantly checked for stability.
Winds, tides, the slightest movement of the sea bed...
You say these radio blackouts have happened before?
Each time a rig has disappeared.
No strange craft in the area? Nothing suspicious?
Difficult to be sure. It was at night.
The radio picked up some strange sound, but as far as we know, the sea was calm and empty.
It may be calm, but it's never empty.
That's right.
I'm Angus Ferguson, McReynold.
My family's been in these parts for generations.
Really?
Well, they told me in the village, Mr McReynold,
that besides being the best piper for miles around, you also have second sight.
Well, I am the seventh son of a seventh son.
You know, that fellow with you, the doctor,
he looks like a man who might see round a few corners himself.
Quite a few.
Oh, now, that's a fine-looking head.
Ah, he owns a 12-pointer.
Brought down by the Duke of Forgill himself.
Gave it to the inn just this last week.
He's a rather strange man, the Duke, isn't he?
Would you think so, miss?
You know, I would deem it a favour if you'd remember that he is the McReynold, my clan chief.
Of course. No, no, it was just that...
Well, after he picked us up in his car, he never spoke a word all the way to the village.
Oh, well, it's true he's now the Duke I remember.
He's been a different man since the oil companies came.
You seem to blame everything on the oil company.
Ah, holy servants.
The servants have left to go and work for them.
Ah, said Forgill, castles are cold, empty house these days.
Wouldn't he care to set foot into myself? That's a fact.
The local people say you had a vision of disaster for the oil company.
Do they now? Mm-hm.
You seem to have done a fair bit of placking in the village, my dear.
Is it true?
I'm no saying, but only bad luck comes to them that settle by Tulloch Moor.
Really? Why?
The moor's a strange, murky sort of place.
When the mist comes down, it's like the steam fare which is cold.
Nobody from these parts will cross the moor after dark.
Oh, Mr McReynold. Now, that's just superstition, surely?
Call it that, if you like.
Well, has anything ever happened to anyone up there?
Aye, aye. There was a man, a foreigner, from the Black Isle, stayed at this very inn.
He went out in the moor, never seen again.
Oh. He left without paying his bills.
Still did he. When did this happen, anyway?
Then there was the case of the Jemison boys, although that was a wee while ago.
OK. What happened to them?
Well, it was, let me see, 1870.
They went out cutting peat and the mist came down.
Donald just disappeared.
They found the older brother, Robert, two days later, wandering about off his head.
His eyes.
His eyes were terrible to see.
For the rest of his life, he never spoke again.
Take my word for it, my dear, there are ancient mysteries here.
Evil spirits haunt Tulloch Moor.
Maybe. But I'm certain of one thing, Mr McReynold.
Evil spirits don't destroy oil rigs.
The rig. I was on the rig.
It's all right, old chap. Don't worry. I'll have you in hospital in no time.
It's too late. We didn't have a chance.
What do you mean? What happened?
I suddenly came out and smashed the rig to pieces.
What did?
If you're interested, the brig's on the quayside watching wreckage being brought ashore.
I thought that'd interest you. He's being very secretive.
If you ask me, he's wasting his time.
Oh, yes, might as well forget about security in Tulloch.
Landlord here's got second sight.
Do you know what he was playing?
Flowers of the Forest. A lament for the dead.
What is that thing you're fiddling with?
It's part of a radio probe system used for checking localised jamming.
Well, what if that gets jammed, too?
Ooh, Fox, in. Harry's been shot.
Strax.
Increased sonic core tone.
Overlay remarse.
Again. Over.
Hibernian control.
Got you very nervous. Loud and clear.
How are things out there? Morale OK? Over.
Everything is fine. Any news of your investigations?
Over.
Nothing much. Brigadier?
Ben Nevis, are you there? Are you there? Over.
Has he said anything? No.
What, nothing at all? No. He's still in shock.
The bullet grazed his scalp.
Harry? Harry, can you hear me?
Harry, it's the doctor. Can you hear me?
Is he all right? No, he's not. He's got a scalp wound.
He should be all right, but he needs time.
Time? Yes, but time is the last thing we have, Doctor.
Another rig's just been destroyed. What?
The Ben Nevis rig, 50 miles west of the Prince Charlie.
40 men aboard, completely vanished.
Same pattern? Exactly the same.
First of all, radio blackout, and then that extraordinary sound.
Now, Mr Huckle's going mad. I'll come back with you.
I'll stay with Harry, then I can call you if there's any improvement.
Good girl.
Harry? Harry, it's me, Sarah.
I think you should let him rest.
He is under sedation, you know. Oh, yes. Yes, of course.
Part of the wreckage from the Prince Charlie. It's been curiously marked.
Look, Mr Benton, nip into the sickbay, will you, and fetch up plaster of Paris.
Plaster of Paris? He'll have some to spare.
OK, Doctor. I'm very curious.
Doctor, do you mind telling us exactly what you're doing?
A little experiment in orthodontology, Mr Huckle.
Orthodontology? Teeth. Teeth. The scientific study of teeth.
It's the cast of a tooth, wouldn't you say?
Teeth? Doctor, you can't be serious.
Teeth are very serious things, Mr Huckle.
Look, let's get this straight.
Are you trying to tell me those rigs were chewed up by a set of giant molars?
Yes. A set of giant molars that can chew through solid steel as easily as paper.
Are you suggesting that we're dealing with some kind of sea monster?
Yes. A monster of frightening size and power.
It's all right, Harry. It's all right.
There's a man on the... What is it?
On the rig. What are you trying to say?
Sister Lammond, I didn't hear you. He's coming round.
Doctor Sullivan? How are you feeling?
Harry, what did you find out? Did Munro tell you anything?
Munro. The man on the beach. The man who was shot.
The rig? Yes. The rig was shaking. Falling.
And then what, Harry? Harry... Keep trying.
I'm going to call the doctor.
It's all right, Doctor Sullivan. You're quite safe.
Your worries are over now.
You're going to be very well looked after.
She says he's recovering. Good. Good. Has he said anything?
He's starting to speak. I think there's something he wants to tell us.
The rig... The rig was smashed to pieces.
Nothing left. Munro in the water, struggling.
It's really cold. I don't suppose...
No, no, I'll be right over. And Sarah...
Better keep his recovery dark for the moment.
Why? Do you think Harry's still in danger from something?
